speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
maintopic: HOUSING
subtopic: UNIVERSITIES IN RECEIPT OF AND ELIGIBLE FOR ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
On September 19 last, during discussion on the second reading of Bill No. 128 to amend the National Housing Act, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate asked if I would place on record in Hansard a list of those universities which have had loans approved under part VIA of the National
Housing Act. I now have this list, and with the permission of the house I shall be glad to have it tabled for inclusion in Hansard.
The hon. gentleman also asked for a list showing all the institutions which would be eligible for such loans. There is, of course, no such definitive list. I thought I had made this abundantly clear when replying to a similar question asked in December of last year, when my answer was recorded on page 1028 of Hansard. However, so as to avoid any further misunderstanding I will again define the meaning of "university" for the purposes of this part of the act. Institutions eligible for loans under part VIA of the National Housing Act are all degree conferring universities or colleges and also other institutions in which courses of full university standard are given although the degree may be conferred by a university with which it is affiliated.
May I have the permission of the house to table the list?

speechtext: To table and print it. Perhaps it would be convenient if it were printed at the point in Hansard where the answer is given. Is that agreed?

The associate committee on the national building code of the national research council considers this design of household fall-out shelters to be structurally acceptable for its intended use for installation in the basements of dwellings, for emergency use only.

There are two aspects of the shelter which diverge, for good reason, from certain of the details of the national building code. The first and most obvious one is that the code stipulates that each room in a house should have a window. It would, of course, defeat the whole purpose of the shelter to put a window in it, and the need for ventilation in the shelter is looked after otherwise by vents which it is recommended be built in appropriate places that will not impair the protective value of the shelter.
The other feature specified in the code which has not been carried into the shelter design is that which states that masonry should not be structurally supported on timber. The shelter uses masonry in the form of concrete blocks as a shielding material. To carry it on steel or on other masonry supports would make the shelter Very much more expensive and more difficult to build. For the emergency purposes for which the shelter is designed and for the period of usefulness that might reasonably be expected for a shelter, it has been determined that, as reflected by the quotation from the associate committee, the design proposed is quite adequate.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I stated last night how astounded and how surprised I was to hear the Liberals proclaim their autonomist faith. We really know them too well to be misled about their sincerity and their sense of responsibility. They know all the arts of make-believe, that I grant; but they surely have exhausted all their acting tricks. Nothing doing now, the people know who they are.
They know that the Liberal party eagerly destroyed the country's constitution while protesting that they were respectful of principles and traditions. We only have to remember the risky initiative of university grants. It constitutes clear enough evidence.
What is happening nowadays? The Liberals are uselessly trying to restore their virginity because a former federalist and centralizer, Mr. Jean Lesage, has placed them in a strange and precarious situation by solemnly stating his deep respect for principles and realities which only yesterday he was despising and treading underfoot.
A frantic centralist in 1949, 1951 and 1954, Mr. Lesage would now be, in 1961, an out-and-out autonomist; and that, shamelessly and even without the elementary tactfulness it would be in order for him to show towards his former accomplices. Flinging his autonomy into their faces, he forgets that the Liberals in Ottawa used to be his friends and associates.
Walking in someone else's shoes, it will be recalled that Mr. Lesage came to Ottawa, in 1960, to bumptiously assert Quebec's rights. He is now opposed to university grants, after having had a hand in the legislation that has put them into effect. He now shamelessly contradicts himself, having finally realized that his own little salvation lies in his being able to show off as an autonomist. He does not care a bit about his associates. That is why they are now like tight-rope walkers. They said so many times that they were in favour of federal grants to universities that today they do not know how to reconcile their former creed with Mr. Lesage's new gospel. For there is no doubt that Liberal members in Ottawa do not share Mr. Lesage's thinking.

We only have to recall the various statements they made, one by one in turn, about
university grants.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record some of the statements I find in volume 3 of Hansard for 1960, in particular the following from the hon. member for Megantic (Mr. Roberge), on page 3315.
I therefore think, Mr. Speaker, that I am entitled to express my humble opinion and to conclude that the central government, or rather the central parliament, has a perfect right to vote grants to the universities, without encroaching on provincial autonomy in the educational field.
Here is another statement, this one from the hon. member for Gatineau, which is found on page 3305 of the same volume of Hansard:
I have always been in favour of university grants.
And now, Mr. Speaker, to add a pleasant aspect to a useful one, I shall quote the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron), whose remarks are found on page 2759 of the same volume of Hansard:
Everybody knows that grants to universities are a Liberal achievement.
It is a Liberal legislation we adopted at the time, that we are approving today, and that we shall continue to approve.
And he added:
We feel that the federal government has not only the right, but the duty, to assist our institutions of higher learning.
As to the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard), he made the following statement, which hon. members will find on page 3550, in the same volume:
There is no possible doubt that the Liberal party was and still is in favour of assistance to universities.
Mr. Speaker, those people should therefore either remain centralists in Ottawa or become autonomists to please their allies in Quebec. In either case, they are inconsistent.
That explains their urge to find in other people instances of their own inconsistency. I shall immediately state, in order to reassure a tortured Liberal conscience, that the Conservative members from Quebec did not break the promise they made to their voters to defend autonomy and the rights of the province of Quebec in general.
Let us recall their stand on Bill C-56. At that time, they voted in favour of a bill which allowed the province of Quebec to pass its own tax legislation without its taxpayers being penalized. For my part, I said at the time that the solution contained in

the bill was of a temporary nature, that it was, after all, a formula of compromise, a fair compromise under the circumstances because it left the door open for a final settlement of the thorny problem created by the Liberal party, when it brought the central power into the forbidden field of education.
At that time I did not hesitate to vote with my party, not only for reasons of political solidarity, but in order to co-operate realistically, without any surrender of principle.
I have always thought, and I want to state it quite categorically, that the problem of the federal government interference in the field of education was not solved for all that. While I had, for the time being, to accept compromise formulas, I have never made a surrender of principles. I would remind those who are looking for inconsistency, of the philosophical notions of end and means.
In my opinion, all the solutions that have been suggested or adopted to this day in order to solve the problem of grants to universities have been and still are only more or less efficient means to reach the goal, that is the progressive but finally total withdrawal of the central government from this prohibited field of education at all levels.
I know that this is not easy and that this problem is closely related to that of tax sharing. Therefore, I appreciate the efforts of the Conservative government to give satisfaction on the one hand to the fierce autonomist demands of the province of Quebec and on the other hand, to the wish of the other provinces which did not understand readily what was at stake in the constitutional fight that Quebec fought alone, or almost alone, in spite of all opposition.
Again I say that the province of Quebec is not like the other provinces. Its characteristics, its stands come from its conception of confederation. One should not be surprised to find that, on certain constitutional matters, the stand taken by the province of Quebec is not the same as that of other provinces. The reason is that things are not yet seen in the same light everywhere and that we must proceed slowly and by steps with those who do not have the same reasons as we have to be autonomists.
This dissimilarity is but the expression of confederation itself, which is a system of compromises that worked unevenly, and it worked only because a lot of concessions were made, often at the expense, unfortunately, of the minority.

It seems that people are afraid to accept the facts and to admit obvious realities, especially this one: that the governments in Ottawa have always been obliged to seesaw.
The coming into power of the Conservative party in 1957 has not brought any change to this basic situation. Confederation remained what it was: a system of compromises the polishing of which is a slow, arduous and very painful process. Will it ever work easily and smoothly? Personally, I have my doubts. But I pay a tribute to the Conservative government which, having inherited a very bad situation, has tried, and successfully, to set things straight and to correct the errors of the past.
After all it cannot be expected to move faster than facts, circumstances and existing situations will allow. The press, which is usually not too friendly towards Conservatives in general, has given credit to the members from Quebec in that respect. It understood the difficult situation in which we find ourselves. But, despite certain appearances which can still lend themselves to confusion, people are beginning to realize that we have fulfilled our undertaking to correct the constitutional situation. We have initiated methods and ways of assertion which have been effective and which should progressively overcome the difficulties brought about by the Liberal regime.
I do not wish to evade the issue rising from the bill before us by confining myself to generalities. I feel this is a worth-while piece of legislation. I think it would be better still if the option clause had been kept in. I will not hold that against the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) as long as he gives me the assurance that the government intends to continue its efforts in order to find a solution which will take into strict account the autonomist rights and demands of the province of Quebec. For we are not free to draw back. The problem of university grants has begun to be dealt with. The government should not, by shilly-shallying, lose the credit they have gained for themselves. Quebec members have no alternative. They need guarantees, while the government's action has only provided a deposit. But we want more than that. Looking at the facts I am led to believe that the government will not fail us, that they will not deceive us, that they will continue and complete the task.

Dominion-Provincial Relations
I know the government is awaiting the Lesage proposals. But he is shy-he is hesitant now, after refusing the offers made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). He seems to be frightened by the consequences of autonomy. In any case, he is in no hurry to grasp the fiscal benefits of these offers, for he would then have the trouble-and quite serious trouble under the circumstances -to say a few words about it to Quebec taxpayers. Moreover, when you see how eager his so-called autonomist government has been to accept the joint plans, after having denounced them in 1960, you no longer have any illusion about the sincerity of his autonomist convictions. His is an awkward task since he must reassure the electors of the province of Quebec, whose votes he obtained under false pretenses, and at the same time, he must prepare his reappearance on the federal scene besides his centralizing associates.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the Quebec members have no choice, regardless of who they are. In his own way, every one of them must keep up the fight for autonomy which was led by Mr. Duplessis. We must admit that it has forced the central government to show a better frame of mind and that it has compelled a new concept of confederation. Indeed, Mr. Duplessis' autonomy was never negative or disguised. He often had to reject bluntly unacceptable proposals. On the other hand, he took the necessary steps.
Many try to minimize the importance of the role he played, to cut down his stature. That is why it is said that his fight for autonomy was inspired by petty considerations. Those people do not want to admit that he was the champion of our rights. He devoted his talents and his energy to the defence and preservation of the work of the fathers of the confederation.
We can rightly ask ourselves: What would have become of the Canadian confederation without him? During the tragic hours of the option, he fought alone and against everyone by refusing to comply with the entreaties of a central government which was anxious to take away from the provinces the rights and privileges they had acquired. He did so only to give his compatriots legal weapons to protect their national heritage. Instinctively, the people of our province understood the meaning of Maurice Duplessis' actions and remained true to him until the end.
Today, as the constitutional situation is becoming less entangled and the central power is led to reconsider sympathetically present and future problems caused by the province of Quebec to other parts of the country, decency requires that we recognize that such an improvement is but the result of the


courageous stand taken by Mr. Duplessis, who showed himself capable placing our constitutional life back on its true course.
His stand brought the central government to repent. Solutions were tried, and then important reconquests were achieved, so that we can now say that he has restored confederation, opened avenues to new researches and shown the way that we think will lead to the political sovereignty of Quebec.
I close my remarks by saying that I have always felt that to work to this end was the responsibility of Quebec members in Ottawa. (Text):

Mr. Speaker, the bill now under discussion is of major importance, not only because it concerns the economies of the ten provinces of Canada but because it also concerns the right of each province to participate equally in the progress and development of this country. It seems unfortunate that a measure of such importance is being discussed on the 173rd day of the present session and in what could be the dying moments not only of the present session but, according to rumours that are circulating, of Canada's twenty fourth parliament.
While speaking in the debate last evening the hon. member for Westmorland made certain remarks which I believe should be answered. First he accused the premier of New Brunswick of suggesting that the other three Atlantic provinces are not poor provinces and that New Brunswick is the only poor province in eastern Canada. I want to say that at no time has the premier of New Brunswick suggested that New Brunswick is the only poor province in eastern Canada. What the New Brunswick premier has done is to bring to the attention of the general public the discrepancy existing in the criteria used under these new arrangements for the distribution of federal grants, which arrangements result in discrimination against the province of New Brunswick.
The hon. member for Westmorland went further and said that the present government of New Brunswick is trying to get sufficient additional money from Ottawa to carry out in full its election promises of 1960. The fact is that the present government of New Brunswick has done more for that province in the first 15 months of its administration than the previous government of the province was able to promise in its eight years in office.

speechtext:
The hon. member took serious exception to the objections raised by the premier of New Brunswick and stated that these objections, to use his own words,

were hardly warranted. The position of the province of New Brunswick in so far as this legislation is concerned was made quite clear in a press release issued by the premier of New Brunswick on Monday of this week. I have here a copy of the premier's statement and I wish to place on record some parts of the statement and comment on others. The release issued by the premier of New Brunswick is in part as follows:
The Prime Minister has recently replied to my letter of July 19, 1961, in which I requested, on behalf of the government of New Brunswick, that a further federal-provincial conference be held to discuss the arrangements to prevail after March 31, 1962. This reply, which has been publicized widely, ignores our request for further discussions, points to our ignorance of the "generous concessions" offered by the federal government, but generally fails to provide any answers to the questions which have been raised, both by letter and in discussion.
For example, we expressed, along with all provinces, very great concern about the lack of flexibility permitted the provinces under the proposed tax collection agreements. The Prime Minister has replied that the new arrangements will permit the provinces-
And this point should be noted, Mr. Speaker,
-"to cultivate the tax fields in the way each province deems fit."
The Prime Minister has made this statement several times, and to this extent I, like him, am reminded of the aptness of a statement made by an ancient public figure, "When I've said it three times, you can consider it the truth".
As further stated in the New Brunswick premier's statement, the facts are that all the provinces have been informed by Ottawa that they are not free to use their own definition of income. The provinces cannot determine the rates of progression; they can take advantage of only those exemptions allowed by the federal government. With regard to the corporation profits tax, should any province or its municipalities impose a non-income tax contrary to federal regulations, there will be a corresponding deduction from the federal payments to the province. I ask the Minister of Finance this question: Is that the way in which to cultivate the tax fields as each province deems fit?
What are the so-called federal concessions? They have already been described as being two in number, and both concessions are very minor. One of these concessions allows the federal government to share substantially the burden of logging taxes imposed by the provinces of British Columbia and Ontario. Of this concession the other eight provinces cannot take advantage. The second concession is to continue the sharing of certain public utility taxes. Such a concession, says the New Brunswick premier, is beneficial only to those provinces which possess private electric power generating companies.
Dominion-Provincial Relations
During the past few months we all know that a great deal has been said about the proposed new arrangements which are before this house for approval, and specifically with regard to their financial effect on various provincial governments. It will be recalled that in his report to the legislature the premier of New Brunswick indicated that the new formula would provide some $600,000 more than the present formula if it were projected to the first year of the new agreement. Since then a number of statements have been made throughout the province of New Brunswick and published in the press to the effect that New Brunswick would receive approximately $2 million to $3 million in extra revenue in the first year of the new agreement, that is to say for the year 1962-63.
I note that the Minister of Forestry is in his seat listening to my remarks. I have here a press clipping from the Fredericton Gleaner under date of September 1, 1961. The heading of this article is "Federal Tax-Rental Scheme Said Not Discriminatory" and it reads as follows:
Federal forestry minister Hugh John Flemming, speaking at a rally of Progressive Conservative supporters in Victoria-Carleton last night, attacked Premier Robichaud's stand that the federal government's tax rental scheme is discriminatory to New 3runswick.
Then in quotation marks appear the minister's own words:
"Those who say, that the tax rental deal is discriminatory to New Brunswick are simply not acquainting you with the facts," he said. "New Brunswick will get $2 million more under the new deal with Ottawa.
"In addition, the Atlantic provinces premiers at Halifax had the responsibility of distributing the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, which were increased from $25 million a year to $35 million a year, or 40 per cent.
I now wish to place on record figures which will clarify such statements once and for all. The figures I am going to quote assume a constant rate of growth in tax yields under each formula so as to make them comparable, and there can be no question that even the federal government and even the Minister of Finance will agree as to the validity of the projections.
The following figures are based on the revenue projections for 1962-63. Under the standard tax yield, New Brunswick under the present formula should receive $9,727,000. Under the proposed formula New Brunswick, again under the standard tax yield, would receive $10,295,000 or a gain of $568,000. But under the equalization payments, under the present formula, New Brunswick will receive $18,484,000 as against $15,698,000 under this proposed formula or a decrease of $2,786,000. Therefore in total, under the present formula New Brunswick would receive $28,211,000

Dominion-Provincial Relations while under the proposed formula it will receive $25,993,000, or a total loss of $2,218,000.
To this it is true-and I wish to be fair- we have to add the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant. Under the present formula the adjustment grant which New Brunswick is to receive will amount to $7,500,000, for a grand total of $35,711,000. Under the proposed formula New Brunswick will receive $10,500,000 in adjustment grants for a grand total of $36,493,000. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, under the proposed formula the net gain to the province of New Brunswick is not $2 million or $3 million in the first year of the application of this act, but is in the vicinity of $782,000.
These figures clearly show the financial impact of each of the three components of the new arrangements as they will apply during the year 1962-63. They also show the reasons, as stated by the premier of New Brunswick, for New Brunswick's objection that such a formula will not make the best contribution to the public interest of that province.
If we consider the standard tax yield the new formula provides, as I have just stated, an additional $568,000 or an increase of nearly 6 per cent over the present formula. However, in order to achieve this result, the present personal income tax percentage accruing to the province will have been increased from 13 per cent to 16 per cent, which means an increase of over 23 per cent in total amount. The same tax increase in Ontario, for example, would raise their revenue by over 14 per cent, or more than twice the rate of 6 per cent allowed to New Brunswick.
This indicates why New Brunswick has stressed the fact that increased emphasis on the yields from the standard taxes discriminates against the poorer provinces with lower tax yields. If we take into consideration the equalization payments under the present formula, the low tax yields of the standard taxes are to a great extent offset by equalization payments which increase in proportion to the increase in the tax yields of the two wealthiest provinces in Canada, namely British Columbia and Ontario. By reducing this growth factor to the national average and by introducing natural resource revenue the new formula produces a decrease in equalization payments, as I stated earlier, of $2,786 million, and reduces the growth potential. Therefore the premier of New Brunswick was right in saying:
This latter statement is axiomatic since it is impossible for this type of "average" to grow as fast as the highest numbers which are included in it.
What are the bases for the new formula which will be applied following the passing


of this bill? The federal government is taking into consideration the natural resource revenue by provinces, and according to figures produced by the dominion bureau of statistics, the revenue for the province of New Brunswick, if the average is taken for the years 1956 to 1958, amounts to $3,978,000, or $7.03 per capita. If the same figures are used for the province of Ontario they amount to $31,381,000, or an average of $5.59 per capita.
Therefore under these new criteria New Brunswick is being looked upon as a province having exceptional revenue from its natural resources, but the fact is that no consideration is being given to the cost to the taxpayers of the province of New Brunswick to maintain and protect those natural resources. This is where there is discrimination.
As the premier of New Brunswick said in his statement, in total the standard taxes, together with the equalization payments, fall short by $2,218,000 of the level that would be achieved under a continuation of the present agreement. It is to cover this shortage that an additional $10 million in grants was awarded to the Atlantic provinces, from which New Brunswick will receive $3 million as its share. Instead of the guarantee, New Brunswick's share of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants will be increased by $3 million, which will be incorporated into the basis for calculating the equalization payments to the Atlantic provinces.
The province of New Brunswick is objecting strongly to this treatment of what was intended as a special and separate payment to the Atlantic region. At the federal-provincial conference and also in letters to the Prime Minister, New Brunswick proposed that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants be kept out of equalization and that the normal guarantee be applied. It is clear that New Brunswick does not receive the full benefit of the increase, since the bulk of it is used to offset the losses resulting from lower equalization payments.
In these objections New Brunswick has been strongly supported by every province in Canada with the exception of Ontario. The representatives of the other provinces made a point of supporting New Brunswick.

speechtext:
Some of them have indicated their support in letters addressed to the Prime Minister which have been made public. In replying to the letter from the premier of New Brunswick with respect to this point, the Prime Minister said only that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grant is separate and "is in no way connected with the basic equalization formula".

I ask how can this be the case when one considers the figures I have quoted and the fact that subclause 4 of clause 4 of this bill, No. C-122, cited as the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements act, specifically says that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants shall be included in determining the tax equalization payment to be paid to a province. There is no question but that the adjustment grant is included, and even less question about the fact that it should not be.
The additional amount provided in this bill is certainly inconsistent with the fiscal requirements of the province of New Brunswick, however measured. Even within the Atlantic region itself there seems to be little relationship between revenue increases and the fiscal needs of each of the Atlantic provinces. I am quoting these figures to give facts, not to complain. I am not complaining about the way the provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island would be treated; I am merely giving facts. Based on similar calculations Newfoundland will receive additional revenue, excluding the special grant of $8 million which they have a right to receive according to the constitution, to the extent of $5.10 per capita; Prince Edward Island, $9.31, and Nova Scotia $2.89. I ask, how do these amounts, particularly the $1.25 for New Brunswick compare with an increase of $2.95 per capita for the province of Ontario, the wealthiest province in Canada?
Hon. members on the government side will say there is no discrimination in the treatment being given to the province of New Brunswick. It is true that the Prime Minister has expressed the hope that upon consideration New Brunswick will recognize "the financial benefits of the new arrangements and the greater freedom and flexibility which they afford". After long consideration with many others no such recognition has resulted, and the premier of New Brunswick was right to make this abundantly clear to the federal government and to the people of New Brunswick. The government of New Brunswick has every right to feel that this new arrangement being forced upon the province is a poor deal for the province of New Brunswick, a poor deal for the government of the province and a poor deal for its people, as well as for the other less wealthy provinces. The provinces are being given no alternative. They must now levy their own taxes upon personal and corporation income, and the result will be to the full advantage of those provinces where the great corporations are located and where personal incomes are at the highest levels. The basis of equalization has been thrown out the
Dominion-Provincial Relations
window, notwithstanding the Prime Minister's
solemn promise to the contrary.
The inclusion of the natural resources income factor will definitely work to the disadvantage of New Brunswick, and as a result of the introduction of this new natural resource basis New Brunswick will receive an additional $1.25 per capita as against additional revenue of $2.95 for the wealthy province of Ontario. Is Ontario in more urgent need of financial consideration than New Brunswick? The facts are that notwithstanding the objections of the premier of New Brunswick, and notwithstanding the serious objections of the seven other premiers who have expressed dissatisfaction with the offer, the provinces have been told by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of Finance, "Take it or leave it".

Before continuing along that line, however, I should like to say that I listened carefully and with a great deal of interest, as I usually do, to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate. I found myself in agreement with him in one particular. I would be the first person to admit that as far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned, without the special adjustment grant of $35 million a case might be made that the eastern provinces had a real grievance. In my opinion, however, that provision completely refutes the speech which was made just now by the hon. member for Gloucester, and I think it refutes to a great extent the assertions made yesterday by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on the question of equalization.
With regard to the adjustment of all provinces to the level of the national average, I acknowledge frankly that I took part in some

Dominion-Provincial Relations conferences in which we brought to the attention of the government, as it was constituted in those days, our feeling that the Atlantic provinces for one reason or another, partly for geographical reasons and partly because of certain commitments made at the time of confederation, should receive special consideration, and that attention should also be paid to the fact that the average national income was considerably higher than the average income in the maritime provinces. At no time did we suggest that attention should be paid by the federal authority to the adjustment of the eastern provinces' income to the level of that of the wealthiest provinces. Our comparison, generally speaking, was made with respect to the national average. I feel that the government today are perfectly justified in taking the national average as the level upon which to base their grants. It seems to me that the special consideration which has been given in that regard is a proper consideration, and I am satisfied to defend that position at any time.
We come now to the provision for stabilization, which I trust will never have to be used. I may say that the previous administration did suggest at one of the conferences,
I	believe it was in 1955 or 1956, that the stabilization feature should be incorporated, or in other words that a province should be protected against a drastic decline in the gross national income as reflected in returns to the central government. It would seem to me that this is a protective feature in so far as the eastern provinces are concerned, and I was very happy when it was decided that this would be the basis on which the new agreements would be drawn up.
In presenting this bill to the house on July
II	the Minister of Finance produced tables indicating the effect of the proposed agreements. I submit that great satisfaction was expressed by some premiers after the conference of last autumn. I suggest that the premier of Newfoundland was very well satisfied. I suggest that he was very happy. I do not know how the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate is going to justify the statements he made yesterday when he meets the premier of Newfoundland in Newfoundland. I found it difficult to reconcile the attitude he took here yesterday with the attitude he should have as the representative of the people of Bonavista-Twillingate. I say this because the hon. member on many occasions has called attention in his own inimitable fashion to the needs of the fishermen in his own riding.
The hon. member also gave credit to the government for the construction of wharves to facilitate the shipment of pulpwood. All

these things indicated to me that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was sincere in his approach, and I had no reason to think otherwise until yesterday. I received a terrific shock when the hon. gentleman addressed us yesterday. I thought he of all hon. members would say that this was about the best thing the government had done for a long time, that this was one of the few things on which he could agree with the government. Instead of that we found the hon. gentleman criticizing the government and saying at the conclusion of his remarks that he found it impossible to support this bill.

Mr. Speaker, we are opposing this bill and voting against it because we think it is a retrograde step and moves Canada's federal-provincial relations away from some very valuable and important principles that had been established over the years.
It has been recognized by successive governments in Canada in recent years that in order to provide for the general prosperity
Dominion-Provincial Relations and welfare of the nation; in order to provide greater equality of services to Canadian citizens within the various provinces, it was necessary for the government to give leadership in bringing about federal-provincial agreements and arrangements that would stabilize the economy, that would provide certain additional revenues to the so-called "have not" provinces and would give the federal government greater opportunity to deal with fiscal measures in such a way as to mitigate widespread unemployment and provide for the general prosperity and expansion of the Canadian economy.
While we in this party have always supported the federal-provincial agreements of the past, we have not hesitated to point out weaknesses that existed and improvements that could be made. We feel that the old agreement was lacking in that it set as the standard for equalization the income from the taxes within the two provinces with the highest incomes, rather than taking the highest income. We think it would have been preferable to attempt to provide the citizens in each province with the services that would flow from the use of revenue in the province where there was the highest income.
Instead there is a retrograde step in this bill before us when it provides that we shall go from a standard of the average within the two highest provinces to the national average. This is a general downgrading of the whole concept of equalization. We think this measure is inferior to the existing system because it is forcing the provinces to go back into the income tax field themselves. This will mean an increase in the variations of income and corporation taxes as between the provinces. This is a return to the tax jungle of bygone days. Also, at least to some extent it does lessen the general effect of federal measures, certainly in the reduction of income tax, to stimulate purchasing power and employment by making certain through this particular measure that provinces have every opportunity, not having signed tax agreements on the original basis, of moving in and taking up, by increasing their own income taxes, any reduction that might have taken place in federal income taxes. This is a backward step, this is retrograde step, this is a piecemeal deal. It is neither fish nor fowl. It does not satisfy the aspirations of the people of any province but it appears to be designed to help, at least in some measure, those governments which are sympathetic to the present administration.

Ontario gains a little by this arrangement. Some of the Atlantic provinces stand to gain a little. But there is a group of provinces which stand not to gain at all. The Prime Minister has complained bitterly in this house over the years-and some of us have helped him- about the unjust deal given by the former administration to the prairie provinces, as well as to other provinces, of this nation. What is in this deal for Saskatchewan? What is in this deal for Manitoba? I ask the Prime Minister where, in this measure, the province of Saskatchewan has a chance to overcome some of the disadvantages imposed on it under the former agreement about which he complained so much? In a speech in the 1957 election campaign, the Prime Minister had this to say:
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation until there is a realization that the federal-provincial matters have handcuffed the provinces of this nation; have denied the municipalities adequate sources of revenue; have placed the provinces and the municipalities in a position where they cannot discharge their constitutional responsibilities or permitting the necessary development in their own territorial confines of the natural resources that there are.

No difficulties that I know about have arisen with regard to relations between the federal government and the government of Saskatchewan. I am not saying there has been trouble about relations with other provinces. But why should the people of Saskatchewan be discriminated against in this measure when the Prime Minister complained so bitterly in the past that a raw deal had been given to that province by the former Liberal administration? In addition, two equalization guarantees are provided. Apparently an attempt is being made through these frequent interruptions to prevent me from saying a number of things I should like to say. As I stated earlier, I did not rise because of the effusions of the hon. member for Assiniboia but I thought some slight reference might be made to his contribution and apparently I made pertinent references because they aroused the hon. gentleman.
I return now to deal in general with the bill before the house and to speak briefly to emphasize certain major points. I shall not recapitulate the history. An explanation of the various items and also of the course followed by the government in this connection was given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in the month of July. Taken together with the publication of the correspondence on this subject, which has been appended to Hansard, and the numerous tables that have been furnished, the Minister of Finance has set forth the whole situation regarding the government's proposals so that they could be understood and judged.
I want to say at once that the purposes of the changes made were to restore once more to the Canadian people the institution upon which confederation is built; in other words, to restore the basic principles of the British North America Act and to assure that the days of centralization in Canada are over. Hon. gentlemen opposite, those who still remain on the front bench, and the governments of their day took under the provisions of the War Measures Act and the powers having to do with war, rights belonging to
Dominion-rrovincial Relations the provinces that were outside of the field of dominion-provincial relations. What they did in this connection was similar to their conduct of invading provincial rights on every possible occasion during the days of war and immediately thereafter. We have decided that the time has come, as I said in 1957, to restore the spirit of the constitution and to return to the provinces their freedom and responsibilities with respect to the imposition of direct taxation on income.
The hon. member for Assiniboia objects strenuously. Those were the happy days, Mr. Speaker.

I can understand why the hon. member for Assiniboia is disturbed. speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
We have restored the inherent principles of the constitution, and this is something we undertook to do. We are ending centralization. We are putting in its place co-operation within the principles of the constitution. This bill represents not merely certain grants to the provinces, or the sharing of tax revenue. It follows in consequence of a series of dominion-provincial conferences; it follows long deliberation and a spirit of give-and-take on the part of both.
We had a number of those conferences. The question was raised whether or not, if the provinces imposed their taxation, there would not be too great an administrative responsibility and cost. We undertook to collect the taxation for the provinces if they chose, and to do so without appreciable cost to them. What we have endeavoured to do in this measure is, I think, tangible evidence of the aspirations of a growing Canada and of the inevitable competition which that brings about between the two levels of government in the use of the basic sources of revenue which are common to them. It reflects, as I see it, the efforts at co-operation between these two levels of government.
I reiterate that we are endeavouring to apply the spirit of confederation, with the sharing of responsibilities and concern for the service and the betterment of the lot of all Canadians wherever they live in this land.
I enunciated our views in this regard at the dominion-provincial conference of 1957, when I said at page 9 of the proceedings:
We believe that this federation cannot thrive in a climate of glaring disparities in levels and standards of service and development as between the several provinces from Newfoundland to British Columbia. Believing in a positive policy, this government intends in co-operation with the provinces to co-operate actively in promoting the development of Canada and all its regions.
This we have carried out by our system of assistance to the provinces under the roads to resources program. This is an example of co-operation to the end that the federal government will assist the provinces and the provinces will co-operate with the federal government in the development of those areas which otherwise would not have been developed for years. I continue:

It is our opinion that positive government is necessary both at the dominion and provincial levels in assuring national development and we are prepared to assist provinces in carrying out their functions where we agree that is necessary and when parliament approves. We are prepared to consider on their merits major projects which will contribute to national development and which are beyond the capacities of any of the provinces.
The example I gave earlier was one of those, the South Saskatchewan dam and others that I mentioned yesterday that I will not repeat now. I went on to say:
In that connection I might refer to three examples. In pursuance of that general plan we have announced a program in respect of power in the maritime provinces. In the speech from the throne reference was made to this government's willingness to recommend to parliament participation with the government of British Columbia in a joint program for the development of the immense potential of the Columbia river.
We do note that the co-operation is not as complete as I would like to see it.
Then I went on to mention the South Saskatchewan dam. I proceeded to outline the general principles in which we believe and the necessity of raising standards in all parts of Canada. I mentioned particularly the Atlantic provinces. When I hear the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), the expatriate from Manitoba and now the proponent of everything for Newfoundland, it surprises me that all during the years that he had this affection he did nothing to bring about anything equivalent to the Atlantic provinces grants to which the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) referred a moment ago. These are the steps that we have taken to elevate standards. I said at that time, as found on page 12:
I believe that we all recognize. .. that the Atlantic provinces as a group are confronted with greater difficulties in public finance than the rest of the nation, if they are to maintain the sort of provincial and municipal services that Canadians generally expect. The taxable capacity of the Atlantic provinces, even in the best of times, is significantly lower than that of the other provinces.
Then I said later:
Recognizing these principles, we are prepared to examine their application and to that end I invite the expression of your views.
In other words, throughout, there was a desire and a declaration in favour of bringing about something that is now being achieved under the policies of the government-the equalization of opportunity in the various parts of Canada and the raising of levels in provinces which did not enjoy the same economic development and present potential as some of the other provinces.
The bill reflects the efforts at co-operation, as I said, in the spirit of confederation. The

fiscal arrangements emphasize the government's desire to make clear both the rights and obligations of all levels of government in Canada as well as to provide through equalization a system of redistributing the fruits of our production on a more equitable basis than would otherwise result.
I am going to refer to the tables to which reference has already been made in order to answer the statement of the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) to the effect that what is being done does not improve the situation of the past and does not carry out the promises of 1957. The statistics answer such loud-spoken statements which are not based on fact and are not borne out by the evidence. I believe that the pattern of the past 15 or 20 years must give way to the requirements of the present. Restore the constitution. Is there any offence in doing that? Are we to alter the provisions of the basic principles of confederation through the medium of tax agreements and the like? Are we to evade those things in the constitution that have been acceptable since 1867? Are we to bring about changes? I agree that changes in the constitution may be necessary, outside of those things that are basic and are constitutional rights possessed thereunder by the province of Quebec and minorities in general which cannot be attacked in any way.
We have endeavoured to bring about a change in the constitution or at least a basis for a change. We have endeavoured over and over again through meetings to ascertain whether it would not be possible, as it should be, to amend Canada's constitution in Canada instead of having to go abroad to the parliament at Westminster. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has done a great deal in this connection. I would point out that, if I understand the record correctly, the one province that stands in the way of this in very considerable measure is the province of Saskatchewan, the leadership of which during the years has spoken of the necessity of having our constitution amendable in Canada. Yet when we are in a position where most if not all of the provinces, I think, are willing to agree, it is the government of the province of Saskatchewan that stands against the fair and reasonable right of amendment as agreed to generally by the other provinces.
I believe there is need for a revised approach to the asumption of responsibilities while maintaining the constitutional distinctions. We want to give the provinces every right to carry out their constitutional responsibilities. It has been nice for some of them to be able to come to the federal government and say, "Give me, give me", while at the same time criticizing the federal government for in-
Dominion-Provincial Relations creased expenditures, and that is particularly the case with regard to expenditures by this government which have been brought about in order to improve the position of the provinces.
It was with these realities and this desire in mind that I proposed to the dominion-provincial conference that the federal government restore to the provinces the freedom to impose and collect taxes on personal and corporate incomes. In order to do this and yet retain the economy and simplicity of a single collecting agency and uniformity in the manner of determining the tax, the bill proposes to authorize the government to undertake on behalf of the provinces the collection of these taxes on personal and corporate incomes provided the tax base in each case is identical with the federal definition. In designing these tax collection agreements, freedom for the provinces to vary their rate of taxation was a prime objective. This freedom provides them with the flexibility to adjust their revenues from year to year in accordance with their needs, and also underlines their independence and direct responsibility.
There has been a great deal said about the promises made by this government. Maclean's magazine has never shown itself to be one of our inveterate friends. Yet I read in the issue of September 23 these words by one of its commentators which I am prepared to accept:
Out of 62 specific pledges made by the Prime Minister during the 1957 and 1958 campaigns, 50 have already been kept or are in process of being discharged.

speechtext: And carried it farther than ever before.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
And, as the hon. gentleman says, with modesty, "carried it farther than ever before". We preserve the principle. We altered the form in order to ensure that the principle would be more generally effective and would carry out the intention of equalization. The principle was a valuable one. The question of its retention was never in doubt for throughout I have consistently stated that it was basic. Although differences have existed and are bound to exist in the methods or formulas by which the principle is to be applied, the purpose or spirit of the principle is not now and has not at any time been in issue. I have made it clear that the principle of equalization is basic. Because a certain formula was evolved some years ago by the former government we do not believe, Mr. Speaker, that such formula is, like the law of the Medes and the Persians, unchangeable. We believe that changes must be made in order to secure its full power and effectiveness, and those changes we have made. In these arrangements we are proposing a revised application of the principle that lays more emphasis upon fiscal need and takes into consideration the prolific revenue derived by some provinces from natural resources as well as the fields of direct tax revenues which have been taken into account previously.
We consider that the present system, based on the three standard tax rates and equalization to the average of the two top provinces, is neither logical nor practical. In some cases it has led to larger payments than could be justified on the basis of fiscal need. It ignored an important source of provincial revenue from national resources. It aimed at an impractical goal in seeking to equalize all to the exceptional top provinces. On the other hand-and I come back to this matter and I will come back to it from time to time-it did not give the needs of the Atlantic provinces in particular sufficient recognition. As the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) pointed out, this was basic to the promises and undertakings of this government. This government, from the very beginning, had a special concern for the fiscal needs of all provinces and, because of the situation in the Atlantic provinces, a special concern for them. We introduced the adjustment grants during the first year of office. It was the federal government that brought this matter before the conference of 1957. In the current proposal


these grants will be increased by 40 per cent. The grants of 1957, which we undertook and brought before parliament and which were passed, are being increased by 40 per cent as part of the broad program. The effect is illustrated in the table by the Minister of Finance on page 7927 of Hansard to which reference has been repeatedly made.
One or two hon. members have played over the same old gramophone record, the same speeches they gave in July last. They gave expression to the same ideas about inadequacy, saying that this government had done nothing to carry out its promises in this connection. I would have thought that the tables themselves would have been sufficient to answer this argument but apparently it is necessary to repeat them. As a whole-and it is always well to take the picture of Canada as a whole-the unconditional grants in Canada in 1956-57 amounted to-and I am speaking always in round numbers-$552 million. I make allowance for the fact that changes were made in the parliament of 1957, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Beni-dickson) indicates, in the manual manner. The amount in 1957-58 was $658 million. They say we have done nothing for the provinces. May I say that the amount in 1960-61 was $841 million and the amount for 1961-62 is $875 million.
If you take into consideration the figures for 1956-57, there will be some who will argue that changes were made by the previous government. But taking the figures at their worst in 1957-58, the result is that there has been an increase of unconditional grants to the provinces of $200 million. When I hear the expressions of some hon. members to the effect that we have done nothing to assist the provinces and to make it possible for the provinces to give greater assistance to the municipalities, may I say the answer is there in the computations as to unconditional grants.
What about conditional grants? As to conditional grants there was no legislative change that I know of in the session of 1957. Therefore we take the figures for 1956-57. In that year there was paid to the provinces in conditional grants an amount of $110 million. The amount in 1960-61 was $430 million, an increase of $320 million. In 1961-62 the amount will be $550 million or, since this government came into power, an increase in assistance to the provinces in the way of conditional grants of $440 million.

they say things like this: "There has been no assistance given to the provinces" because they exchange their prejudices and they think they are thinking. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Hospital insurance is overlooked.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
One hon. gentleman mentioned hospital insurance. Yes, it is true that the Liberals brought it in but we pay for it. There is no doubt about that fact and it has to be included in that amount.
Now for the payments to provincial institutions. The amount payable to provincial institutions in 1956-57, for university grants and grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal property in 1956-57, was $25 million. In 1960-61, it was $43 million and for 1961-62 it will be $44 million. Again there is a tremendous increase.
In the face of these tremendous increases these hon. gentlemen opposite, by simply repeating statements which they must know are not borne out by the facts, believe that the Canadian people can be fooled into believing that we have not improved the position of the provinces very greatly since 1957.
I am not going to go over all of the provinces but I must mention Newfoundland even in the absence of the hon. member, although there are others who have a representative position here from that province and therefore it will permit me to refer to it. Newfoundland, which was spoken of in lachrymose tones by an hon. gentleman now not with us, in 1956-57 received $17 million, in 1957-58 received $19 million and in 1961-62 the estimate is $38 million. Those amounts are in connection with unconditional grants. In conditional grants it received $6,500,000 in 1956-57 and the amount for 1961-62 is $23 million. He said, "Well, we have not got anything. We have not received that consideration which we should have received". I simply point out those facts, Mr. Speaker! In addition to that, there are payments for the benefit of provincial institutions. These were $415,000 in 1956-57 and today the estimate is $780,000. So I could go on through the record.
I now come to the province of New Brunswick, to which some reference was made. However, I do not think I have to cover the figures there because they were dealt with amply and carefully by the Minister of Foresty (Mr. Flemming).
Dominion-Provincial Relations
Then I come to the province of Saskatchewan. After all, I could not but be touched by the words of the hon. member for Assiniboia. He spoke with everything but authority.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: How true.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: He said this is how serious the situation was. I have his exact words here. He said, "This is a retrograde step, a backward step and it is most unfair to the province of Saskatchewan."

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Let me read the record. Unconditional grants for 1956-57 were $29\ million; for 1957-58, $35 million; for 1960-61, $42 million; and approximately the same for the present year. Conditional grants were $7,700,000 in 1956-57, and in 1961-62 they are $27 million. I do not understand the mentality of anyone who, knowing those figures, would make the type of suggestion that the hon. member made here today, that Saskatchewan for some reason was being penalized and we had done nothing to improve the situation of Saskatchewan since 1957 over what had been the prevailing condition during the years prior to 1957. In the field of payments for the benefit of provincial institutions the figure was $1,165,000 in 1956-57, and in 1961-62 it is a total of $2,140,000. I place those figures on the record simply for the purpose of having objective consideration given to the rather- and I understate the situation when I say this-distorted view given by the hon. gentleman.
There was another province that was being discriminated against, as I remember. I have dealt with Newfoundland; New Brunswick was dealt with by the Minister of Forestry and I have covered Saskatchewan. Then Alberta and British Columbia were mentioned. As far as Alberta is concerned, the total amount of unconditional grants, conditional grants and payments for the benefit of provincial institutions amounted in 1956-57 to $49 million; in 1957-58 it amounted to $62 million, and in 1961-62 the figure is $103 million.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: How much under the new agreement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I find it difficult to understand that the hon. gentlemen would make these kind of loose, idle and disorderly statements. Certainly they are vagrant observations which have no foundation in fact.
Now we come to British Columbia. I think it was the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Regier), the financial man, who dealt with this during the month of July.

Dominion-Provincial Relations He spoke, too, of how British Columbia was another of these forgotten provinces. The total amount paid to British Columbia in 1956-57 in unconditional grants, conditional grants and payments for the benefit of provincial institutions was $77 million; for 196162 the figure is $150 million.
These are the increases that have taken place during a period of four years. I think they emphasize that this government has carried out its promise to give the provinces a new deal; to give to the provinces moneys which they in turn may pass on in whole or in part to the municipalities. We have made that very clear.
Besides this type of thing there are the other plans that we have announced and which are in effect. There is the assistance to technical education. That is something that affects every part of this country. This is a tremendous benefit. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) brought this measure into being whereby we give to the provinces 75 per cent of the costs of building technical schools and providing the equipment.
These hon. gentlemen say there has not been a new deal. Well, Mr. Speaker, I will be glad to hear them argue that question any time when the opportunity is at hand and I will give even greater detail than I have given up to now. This table shows strikingly how the total of the grants to the provinces under these new arrangements and the revenues they can procure by utilizing the room to be left to them under the new plan-I refer to the table at page 7927 of Hansard-exceed very substantially the benefits they would have secured under a continuation of the position under the 1957 act before the amendments this government put forward. Moreover, in addition to the improvement reflected in this table for the year 1962-63, there will be further improvement in the following years due to the increasing federal withdrawal from the individual income tax field.
Mr. Speaker, there are other matters that I thought I might put before the house, but I will leave them to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to deal with. I did feel, however, that I had a responsibility simply to place the record before the house; not the expurgated record, not the self interpreted record, but the facts. On the basis of facts and on that record I think all of us have reason to agree with the summary made by the Minister of Forestry, with provincial experience behind him, that this government has indeed been serious, and more than serious, has been effective in raising the standards of the provinces, and in the years ahead under the new plan as I understand it, no province will receive less than it is receiving today.


Does not this reveal the actual facts of what we have done? There are some who believe that because this rental plan was evolved in the fertile mind of one who is not now with us-at least he has been given the honour of having produced it-that therefore it should be unchanged. The changes that have been made hurt no one. The changes that have been made will actually assure to each of the provinces at least the amount they are receiving today; that amount, as I have shown, being tremendously greater-two, three, four, five times greater-than the amounts that were being paid to the provinces either conditionally or unconditionally in 1957.
On examination it will be seen that the total of federal contributions to the provinces, certain payments to institutions normally the responsibility of the provincial governments and tax abatements made to facilitate the raising of provincial revenues, has risen-and I summarize-from $689 million in the fiscal year 1956-57 to an estimated $1,470 million for the current fiscal year. This is a prodigious increase in the amounts granted from the federal budget to the provincial budgets of this nation. It is not going to be lower under the new plan. Had it not been for the change of government, where would the Atlantic provinces have been? Where would have been several provinces which have received assistance to provide for policies of expansion and development? Where would they be in reference to the development of power in the maritimes, the potential power and irrigation in the province of Saskatchewan and the possibilities of the province of British Columbia, if agreement can be secured, as apparently it had been verbally secured prior to the signing of the Columbia treaty in 1961? These increases, as I have pointed out, have been related to a much better assessment of the fiscal needs of the provinces than ever before as well as to the needs and desires of the Canadian people for various worth-while services in respect to which payments and grants have been made to provincial institutions.
I shall not try to describe the variety and scope of this program, ranging as it does from such small but important items as assistance toward the construction of fishing vessels, which has recently been substantially improved, to such huge programs as those for hospital and diagnostic services. All these programs, as well as the fiscal arrangements themselves, are designed to assist all the provinces in providing for their citizens the best services and facilities which Canada can afford and the Canadian people will support.
I think that no one who is fair minded, no one who is not blinded by party prejudice or

local considerations, can fail to appreciate that the burden on the federal treasury has been very heavy indeed as a consequence of these programs to assist the provinces. When people speak about deficits, due regard should be paid to the increases which have been made in other fields, realizing that those deficits have in large, in overwhelming measure, been the result of the fact that for too long the people have waited for action. They demanded that there should be action and we have tried to carry out that action to a degree which, I think, the Canadian people will appreciate. The Canadian people, whenever the opportunity comes will not, I am sure, listen to the whiners and the wailers but will realize that here has been solid achievement on behalf of all Canadians.
I believe that this bill, which provides for a considerable increase in the provincial sharing of the personal income tax in addition to an improved equalization formula and increased Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, constitutes a generous arrangement with the provincial governments.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Somebody said "They want more". I can understand that, Mr. Speaker. Did you ever know of anyone to whom something had been given who did not want more? That is human nature. When the opposition was in power, the provinces said they were not getting enough. We increased the amount, two, three, four times, five times. And, naturally, they said: Don't we get more than this?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Frost, particularly, complains about this government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
So far as Mr. Frost is concerned, I am glad to see some recognition today. That is the Liberal way-always to recognize ability when a person is about to give up office. Those were not the hon. gentleman's words a year or two ago; but reformation, however late it comes, always means forgiveness.
The proposed agreements to collect taxes for the provinces without charge, thereby safeguarding the simplicity and uniformity of our tax system means that greater freedom will be left to the provinces to set their own rates of taxes. I am sure this is something which serves the interests and convenience of the taxpayers. I am confident that the new arrangements will make it possible to meet the problems of disparity in provincial revenues more fairly and realistically than in the past. Greater recognition has been given to the persistent fiscal disabilities of the Atlantic provinces. The preservation and extension of the fundamental principles of freedom for provinces to tax as they see
Dominion-Provincial Relations fit, of equalization based on broader determination of fiscal need and the fuller recognition of fiscal disabilities peculiar to the large eastern segment of Canada will contribute to the financial strength and independence of the provinces and to equality of opportunity for Canadians throughout Canada. It will lead to a restoration of the constitution to its basic concept, to the maintenance of provincial rights; to the assurance, by federal aid, that those who live in provinces which are underprivileged economically by comparison with others will have their standards raised. It is in the spirit of fair and equal treatment, within the framework of our constitution, that this bill has been presented, and I hope it will receive the support of the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
This debate began very quietly with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) saying very little, contrary to his habit in the house. I understand that he had made a long trip, and perhaps that had something to do with his reticence in the house when this matter came before us.
However, during the course of the afternoon the debate seems to have warmed up, particularly since the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming) and then, later, the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) decided to enter the discussion. The hon. member for Royal objected to a statement made by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Robichaud) to the effect that the Robichaud government had done more in 15 months than the former provincial administration had done in eight years. I do not know whether that is the case or not, because I am not familiar with New Brunswick politics, but I do know that if this was the language used by the hon. member for Gloucester he was using precisely the kind of language which the Prime Minister and his followers use consistently when they say that in the last three or four years they have done more than was done by the previous administration in 22 years.
The hon. member went on to say that in New Brunswick, now, they are cutting the ribbons in connection with projects started by the former administration. Well, for the last four years that is all hon. gentlemen on the other side of the house have been doing. They have been cutting the ribbons of a multifarious number of projects started by the former administration and, very often, they have not even had the courtesy to invite those who had something to do with those projects-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

As I listened to the Prime Minister, particularly toward the middle and the end of his speech, the feeling grew within me with increasing intensity that perhaps there is an election in the air.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

speechtext: The Prime Minister went on to say that this is the end of centralization, that we are concluding centralization and substituting co-operation. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
There was no centralization in the tax rental agreements. Even during the war they were voluntary. Quebec never accepted after the war. When in the early 1950's Quebec introduced double taxation the St. Laurent government provided for a deduction from the federal tax the same year and then introduced equalization which removed any shadow of disability between the agreeing and non-agreeing provinces. Again in 1957 the equalization system increased payments to the provinces by $100 million, more than anything yet done by the present government in the tax sharing field.
[Mr. Speaker.)

I wish to remind the Prime Minister that during the campaign of 1957 he and his followers claimed that under the tax sharing agreements negotiated by the former administration which will expire on March 31 next the provinces had been "forced into a starved condition". Those were the words the Prime Minister used. He promised to assure fairness to all.
As the house knows, during the campaign of 1957 Mr. Frost supported the Prime Minister's policy, as did the Frost government in Ontario, and said that if the Conservative party was elected Ontario would receive an additional $100 million annually out of the federal treasury. What is happening now? As I said, Ontario will receive $18 million more and has to impose a tax of 3 per cent in order to meet the difference.
Here is the situation. The government pretends that this is a better scheme than the one which existed before. Mr. St. Laurent in his statements in the house and outside never pretended at any time that the formula which he brought forward was perfect. He said it could be improved but he also said that under the circumstances it was the best formula that could be found. I am convinced that the formula contained in this legislation is not as equitable as the previous one.
What are the facts? The government pretends that the formula contained in this legislation is a better one. It is better for Ontario, by $18 million-

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: They thought they had a wink for $100 million.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

But what is the situation in Quebec, Manitoba and Saskatchewan? All three are in the same position. The government's formula is so bad it did not dare apply the formula to those provinces. Instead of applying this fine new formula to those provinces the government will have those provinces remain under the existing law. In other words for those three provinces the present law is better than the government's new scheme, as is clearly demonstrated in this bill.
For British Columbia and Alberta there is an actual reduction and those provinces will be worse off under the new scheme than under the existing law. As the Minister of Forestry said before the luncheon adjournment, the Atlantic provinces would have been so much worse off under the new scheme

that the government had to add another $10 million to the Atlantic provinces grants to make up the difference. But this device created new inequalities within the Atlantic provinces themselves as the hon. member for Gloucester so clearly pointed out this morning.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
