maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
To sum up, there is no improvement whatever in the new equalization formula for nine of the ten provinces. I ask, Mr. Speaker, whether this is the way to promote the national unity and harmony which the Prime Minister promised in 1957? So far as Quebec is concerned there is absolutely no improvement. The minister has refused to indicate whether there is any prospect of improvement as he did by not answering the question put to him by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in which the minister was asked to produce in this house a comparative table which would illustrate the situation under the new formula as compared with that under the old. Obviously such a comparison would not be helpful to the government.
This is the great new deal for the provinces and municipalities which the Prime Minister promised in his opening campaign speech at Massey Hall on April 26, 1957 when he said:
We believe there can be no national unity in this nation until there is a realization that the federal-provincial matters have handcuffed the provinces of this nation: have denied the municipalities adequate sources of revenue: have placed the provinces and the municipalities in a position where they cannot discharge their constitutional responsibilities or permitting the necessary development in their own territorial confines of the natural resources that there are. We believe the provinces and municipalities must have the financial resources to carry out those responsibilities. We believe in the federal system of government. We believe that its preservation is essential to Canadian unity. We believe the federal system is today being challenged by the centralization complex of the St. Laurent government and that a healthy division and balance of revenues as between the federal and provincial governments must be assured.
We intend to form a government to immediately convene a dominion-provincial conference to bring about a settlement of these problems, not in the spirit of arrogant domination as displayed by the present government, but in the spirit of unity and amity and with mutual tolerance and respect.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
The Prime Minister nods in affirmation of what he has said. I ask if it was evidence of national unity when, following the conference here, practically all of the premiers, except perhaps one, declared their inability to abide by the proposals put forward by the present government and voiced their dissatisfaction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I state, in the light of what is being said here and what has happened in the form of this legislation, the federal government puts forward this proposal which was set out at the conference last February and in a spirit of, I say to you, "arrogant domination" they have refused to change at all, and what is more, they have even refused to confer again with the provinces that have asked for a conference. They have refused to confer even though seven premiers expressed strong opposition to this scheme and several of them, including the premier of the province of Quebec, have asked for another conference.
In order to support that contention I intend to put on Hansard portions of the letter which the Quebec premier wrote to the Prime Minister. The letter from Premier Lesage is dated July 13, 1961, and reads as follows:
(Translation):
The Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, P.C., Q.C. Prime Minister of Canada,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear sir:
My colleagues and I have dutifully given close consideration to your letter of June 16, 1961, in which you set forth the federal government's intentions with regard to the questions raised during the recent federal-provincial conferences and, more particularly, the one which was held in Ottawa on February 23 and 24 last.
The province of Quebec has passed its own laws in the matter of personal and corporation income tax. I have no intention of proposing to the legislature that the care of collecting those taxes be entrusted to the Department of National Revenue. For that reason, I shall refrain from commenting on the collection agreements suggested.
With respect to the equalization formula, the guarantee offered and the gradual widening of the taxation field reserved to the provinces in the matter of personal income tax, I must point out once again that the effect of widening the taxation field is illusory for us, to all practical purposes, since what is given to us with one hand is taken away with the other, due to the decrease in equalization.
Personal and corporation income tax is already a heavy burden for our taxpayers. Therefore, our government will not be able to avail itself of a freer hand in the taxation field without maintaining or increasing double taxation.
You will understand that my colleagues and myself were bitterly disappointed by your letter. As I pointed out in Ottawa, the province of Quebec is in full expansion and needs additional revenues. In order to reach the national average, its expenditures, according to D.B.S. figures should be materially increased in the important fields of education, health and communications. Those are priority requirements and only through an increase in the revenues at our disposal shall we be in a position to carry out our obligations under the constitution.

Dominion-Provincial Relations (Text):
I jump over several paragraphs (to come to this concluding one.
(Translation):
Under the circumstances, it is urgent that another conference be held in order to seek an agreement and to see that no such serious misunderstanding be allowed to subsist.
I have no objection to quoting the answer given by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his letter; the only thing to which I would object is what I have noticed going on between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). I am not saying this to be at all mean toward the Prime Minister.
However, I do congratulate him for his contribution at that time and, with his permission, I should prefer not to read his letter, first because it is long and second, because it is printed in Hansard where he can easily find it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the Minister of Finance takes part in this debate, I should like to supplement what

members on this side of the house have had to say about this measure. I join with my colleague the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) to put in perspective some of the things which have been put improperly in attempted perspective today by the Prime Minister.
It must not be forgotten that one of the assurances given by the Prime Minister in the election of 1957, as we were reminded today by the hon. member for Laurier, was that if his party was elected to office and he was made Prime Minister, he would end once and for all the unfair situation that prevailed in fiscal matters between the federal and provincial governments. It will be recalled that he associated that promise with the statement that not later than the month of September, 1957 a conference would be held with the provinces to resolve this question. Well, parliament was called together in the fall of that year. This government sat to your right, Mr. Speaker, for the first time in the autumn of 1957. No conference had been called, as was promised by the government of the day. Hansard records persistent interrogation of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Finance asking when a conference of the provinces was going to take place. Well do I remember particularly reminding the Prime Minister of the promise he made in that regard at St. Patrice de Beaurivage in the province of Quebec. But, Mr. Speaker, no conference took place until after prodding by members of the Liberal party. At the end of October we were told by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Flemming) that the provinces were going to meet with the federal government some time in the month of November We all remember what took place then. The conference met, it is true. Every provincial premier made his declaration of policy and intention and made his requests to the government, a government that had promised to resolve this question for all time.
After the provinces had stated their case and the Minister of Finance his preliminary statement, and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) had expressed solicitous phrases of welcome to the capital of our country, the conference adjourned. No action was taken, no policy statements were formulated, no agreement was entered into between the provincial and federal governments in November, when they first met. The communique issued after that conference clearly indicated that it was understood that the conference would be reconvened in the month of January. We were told that in this house by the Minister of Finance. Well, what happened? Before many days in the month of January had expired the Minister of Finance rose and.

instead of announcing the date that the conference would be reconvened, gave to the house the terms of a telegram which had been dispatched to the provincial premiers and in which the government, a government that was going to sit down at the table and have joint exchanges with the provinces on these complicated and highly important matters, laid down to the provinces its policy: "We are going to give you so much money; these are our terms and this is the situation whether you like it or not". Those were not the elegant words used by the Minister of Finance but I am paraphrasing the thought.
We all remember too that the amounts of money set forth in the telegram were later proven to be erroneous and not in harmony with the facts. In other words, the mathematical calculation of the minister in that telegram was proven to be erroneous. I later charged, and I repeat the charge now, that that telegram sent to the provinces was prepared by an official in the treasury of the government of Ontario and not by an official here in Ottawa.

In any event, the fact is that the provinces were not called back and every premier expressed his indignation in public. Premier Stanfield of Nova Scotia did so as did Premier Roblin of Manitoba and all the other premiers joined these two to express their displeasure and indignation at the high-handed manner in which federal-provincial fiscal relations 90205-6-568i
Dominion-Provincial Relations were being treated by a government that was going to resolve this problem once and for all.
We know what took place then. An election took place. That was the reason for the telegram. It was not because the government was anxious to make a deal. It was because they were on the verge of an election. They knew that if the Prime Minister went to western Canada, particularly to Manitoba, the Prime Minister, in the face of the negative attitude taken by the federal government in November, would have been greatly embarrassed, especially in Saskatchewan and Manitoba by the state of federal-provincial fiscal relations at that time.
We talk now about the principle of equalization. Let us not forget the attitude of the government including the Prime Minister and more particularly the Minister of Finance. We know that the former government under the leadership of Mr. St. Laurent, having in mind the unequal conditions that prevailed with regard to tax revenues available to the provinces, embarked upon the principle of equalization based upon the direct tax revenues of the two wealthier provinces. That was a principle which the provinces recognized as a satisfactory way of providing for the inequities existing under our federal system, so far as a number of the provinces were concerned in relation to the two wealthier provinces. When we came back after the election of 1958-

speechtext: You are changing it in your speech.

speechtext:
My hon. friend says I am changing it. If I am changing it, that is something my hon. friend ought to recognize, namely that there is a value in changing one's position from time to time, particularly if it is wrong.
The Prime Minister today made much of the conditional grants given to the maritime provinces. My hon. friend can point right now to an increase, dollarwise, in current grants to the provinces. But this is not the test. The test of this legislation and of the principle behind it is this: What is the permanent structure on which will be based future grants to be made to the provinces by the federal government? To say that this particular year there is being given to the Atlantic provinces the sum of X dollars more than was given three or four years ago does not in any way meet the issue that is involved in this discussion. Of course there are increases but those increases, based on the present principle of grants made to the provinces, will in ensuing years result in a financial situation to the provinces less favourable under the present formula than would have been the case under the formula for which the present bill provides a substitute. That is the incontestable fact.
For instance, let us consider the province of Newfoundland and the maritime provinces generally. They are not treated as generously as the Prime Minister seems to suggest. We must not forget that Prince Edward Island, as well as Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are full partners in confederation as of course are the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The government talks of equal treatment because of its forced adherence now to the principle of equalization. That principle of equal treatment is not observed in the tax arrangements as far as Prince Edward Island is concerned, for instance. Under the new proposal the total increase in revenues to be received in the province of Prince Edward Island will be $3 per person. The annual increase to my own province of Ontario in the same period will be $6 per person. In the face of this how can the Prime Minister talk about fairness to all the provinces?
A moment ago I was talking about the principle of equalization. The application of the principle of equalization ensures, I repeat, that the direct tax revenue from the three sources of taxation for every province, on a per person basis, would equal the direct tax revenues of the two wealthiest provinces. That principle is vital, I repeat, to Prince Edward Island and to all the provinces that

are economically less well endowed. But I repeat that it has been jeopardized by the new arrangements now being embodied in the bill, the principle of which we are now discussing, because the national average has been substituted for the average of the top two provinces.
I say that does not fully give to the provinces-the so-called have not provinces, the so-called less developed provinces-the same benefits as those given under our application of the principle of equalization. If our application of the principle of equalization were to be applied the treasury of the province of Prince Edward Island would receive an additional half million dollars per year on top of the moneys now extended to it. That is the situation. Yet we have the Prime Minister repeating words which the Minister of Finance has put in his mouth and which we know do not represent the true situation.
However, we have not had the whole story. It is connected with one of the most important political personalities in our country. I refer to Premier Frost. In April 1957, in the opening campaign meeting in connection with the elections of that year, Premier Frost appeared on the platform with the present Prime Minister. We all remember the assurance given by those two hon. gentlemen to the people of Canada and to the province. On that occasion, Mr. Frost put his hand on the shoulder of the present Prime Minister, then leader of the opposition, and said, "This is my man. Elect this man and Ontario will get from the federal government what Ontario has not been able to get from the St. Laurent government. We want at least another $100 million in order to discharge our obligations. This amount we cannot get from the present federal government. Elect this man, my friend John, and Ontario will get a new deal". That was an assurance given by the premier of Ontario. The Prime Minister did not say, "Oh, I cannot commit myself to assurances like these. This is a very large sum of money. I must take into account the situation in Manitoba and the situation in Saskatchewan. I must realize that if I am elected I am going to be the prime minister of all of Canada."

My hon. friend says, "For a long time". All my hon. friend does is to make interjections like that. Because of this he will not be here for a long time.
In any event, that was the promise made by those two gentlemen. What is the situation? After the election of 1957 Mr. Frost wore out the red carpet from Toronto to the east block with his visits in an attempt to get a new deal from the Prime Minister,
Dominion-Provincial Relations his friend John, the man whom he had recommended to the people of Canada. He could get nowhere with the Prime Minister because the Prime Minister could get nowhere with the Minister of Finance. That was the reason. It was not until two years had elapsed that the premier of Ontario, his patience exhausted, said that his first responsibility was to the province of Ontario and that because he could not get what he wanted out of the then federal government, now headed by the present Prime Minister, he would have to change his formula. We know what that change amounted to. Instead of the premier of Ontario asking for $100 million or $118 million, when he came here to Ottawa on the second last occasion he raised his ante and he said, "Since I was not able to get my original amount,"-and, he might have added, at least in parenthesis, what had been promised at that Massey Hall meeting in April of 1957-"I now must ask for $500 million. In no other way can I, as premier of Ontario, discharge my responsibilities and see that schools are built, provide for the building of highways and the like". As a result of that last conference Ontario did not get what it wanted, of course. Ontario got much less than the $500 million, and not anything like the full amount of the $100 million originally asked for.
What is the result? The result is that in the province of Ontario today there has been imposed a sales tax which has aroused the people of Ontario as very few tax imposts in that province have done.
Mr. Pallet!: A tax fully supported by the leader of the Liberal party in Ontario.

He does not say, "Blame the Minister of Finance" in these words-

Dominion-Provincial Relations

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.

-will be made known. We hope we will learn the nature of the conversation between the premier of Ontario and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker) on the day before the premier of Ontario announced, with understandable reluctance, his decision to leave Ontario politics. Some have even suggested he is not going to leave politics, that he is going to come to Ottawa and take up an appointment in another institution of this parliament. It may be that he hopes in that capacity to exercise a greater influence on this government than he did as premier of the province of Ontario.
The government is confronted with this background to this bill. It must not be forgotten that this government's policy in this particular is most regressive. When one thinks of the complicated financial structure that exists in this confederation of ours, with ten provincial governments and one federal government, a government which since the war has rented certain tax fields from the provinces, corporation taxes, income taxes and succession duties; when one realizes the confusion that prevailed before the present arrangement and the demands made by responsible people of all classes in this country almost since the beginning of this century up to the Rowell-Sirois report in 1941, and what followed that report; and the decision of a former minister of finance, Mr. Ilsley, to bring about this new formula in connection with these tax fields, all one can say in the light of all this history is that we are now embarking legislatively on a program that is most regressive. Some day this government will regret the step it is taking.
It may relieve the government of political embarrassment. They may now more successfully resist some of the requests and demands being made by the provinces, but as a result of this bill which we are shortly going to discuss-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: Discuss?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext: We are discussing it now.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS AGREEMENTS RESPECTING TAX COLLECTION, ANNUAL GRANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
As a result of this bill, the details of which we are shortly going to discuss, this government has embarked on a course that is regressive and

is going to encourage provinces to enter fields of taxation-which it will be within their right to do-which will place on the Canadian taxpayer a serious burden. After all, all the moneys that come to governments on all levels originate in only one source, and that is the Canadian citizen who, out of his hard work provides governments on all levels with the financial resources to carry on the projects of government.
Premier Robichaud announced yesterday in New Brunswick that as a result of this bill he is going to have to go out and get $2J million more. There is talk now of the provincial legislature being called for the purpose of enabling that body to consider additional forms of taxation to be imposed on the people of New Brunswick, just as a similar situation has developed in the province of Ontario and as it will develop in other provinces.
The federal government has obligations in national defence, social welfare and the like. In the latter field we have not stopped. There is still a great deal to be done. But I say that this government, by the regressive step it is taking, in this measure, is putting one of the greatest halting blocks to further social reform in this country, because it is imposing obligations on the Canadian people that will come from further imposts by the provinces, and which our people will find it increasingly difficult to bear.
The Prime Minister did not say a word about that. He simply referred to the increases in the conditional grants since this government came into office. Incidentally, these increased conditional grants were based on grants originally provided for by Liberal governments under Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. St. Laurent. The Prime Minister referred to the increases in hospital insurance payments and to other conditional grants. Let it not be forgotten, that long before this government came along, and sometimes against the opposition of its supporters in this house, grants were made to the provinces in the field of social welfare by the former government in a wide area of social interest. When we compare what was paid out in old age pensions, old age assistance, blindness allowances, family allowances, unemployment insurance and disability pensions, and the like, by the former government with the allocations made during the past four years, it is no wonder that we marvel at the daring of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in suggesting today that the increases in the social services represent the unique interest of this government in social welfare. Of course, these are obligations which would have to be continued by this government. But the Prime Minister said nothing about
Dominion-Provincial Relations the authorship of these measures; he said nothing about the antecedent situation and how the structure on which these measures are based was provided.

Dafoe, and the late Newton Rowell, of men like Frank Scott, Dr. Skelton and others who over a period of many years laid the groundwork in this country for the principles embodied in the recommendations of the Rowell-Sirois report, which was later carried out in part under the former administration when Mr. Ilsley was prime minister.

Let us see what there is in substance in these criticisms. We are told that there is some discrimination in the formula which has been put forward in this bill, that there is an attempt being made to favour provinces with Conservative provincial administrations and to give less than equal treatment to provinces with administrations of another political stripe. That statement just is not true. This is a formula which applies to all the provinces. We have not doctored the formula. We have not put forward a formula which applies to some while another applies to others. This bill contains one formula applicable to all the provinces.
I shall make a qualification as regards favouritism. It is that this bill favours four provinces, and those are the four Atlantic provinces. It does favour them. We admit that. It favours them to a degree that no fiscal legislation in the history of this country has ever favoured any province. When it comes to a charge of favouritism in that respect, we plead guilty and we put our case before the house.
This is definitely a Conservative measure. Atlantic provinces adjustment grants were never heard of before this government came into office. This afternoon we heard from the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin). We heard from the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). We heard at great length yesterday


from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate (Mr. Pickersgill). These were all members of the former administration. Their formula, the 1956 formula which came into effect in April, 1957, was: 10 per cent of the individual income tax for the provinces. These are the 10 per cent men. Look at them -10 per cent written all over them.

In 1957 when the electorate passed upon the record of the former government and the policy which was offered to them by the present Prime Minister, the people made their choice and hon. members opposite know perfectly well in their hearts, notwithstanding their hollow blustering today, that the promise made by the present Prime Minister before that 1957 election was carried out within a matter of months of his taking office. I wish now to touch briefly on the subject of what have been called the guarantees. It is an essential part of the formula in this bill that, in the first place, no province shall receive less, in dollars, than it is receiving this year, 1961-62. It is equally a fact and a provision of this bill that no province in which the yield from the standard taxes and the revenues from resources is less than the national average will receive less than it would have received if the present formula were continued into the new period.
There are firm guarantees that undergird the fiscal position of the provinces. These are an essential part of the formula presented in this measure. This undergirding of the fiscal position of the provinces does not stop there because this bill, in compliance with the earnest pleas made by the provinces, does write into the arrangements a provision in relation to the stabilization of revenues on the 95 per cent basis that has been requested by


the provinces. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there are guarantees of the firmest kind here, and we have here the most generous provision that has ever been made or that any parliament in this country's history has ever been invited to make for the assistance of the provinces and the buttressing of confederation in this country.
We are asked, sir, to confer again, to call another dominion-provincial conference. This request is echoed in this house by hon. members who have been busying themselves for the last several years in deriding the numerous dominion-provincial conferences that we have called. There have never been as many dominion-provincial conferences at any time as there have been in the past several years. The present formula is the outcome of three dominion-provincial conferences.
Hon. members opposite have been asleep. The first of those conferences was held, July 25 to 27, 1960; the second from October 26 to 28. 1960, and the third on February 23 and 24 of this year. There have been three plenary conferences with relation to this coming period and the fiscal arrangements that are to govern in this period.
Hon. members opposite have engaged in such exaggerations. Actually the requests in this respect have come from only three provinces. We have heard the views of those provinces on every feature of the present proposals. There is nothing in this bill that has not already been discussed in one form or another at the conferences, so there is nothing that can be accomplished by another conference except repetition. Therefore a conference, as the Prime Minister has pointed out in his very courteous and understanding letters in reply to those letters from provincial premiers which are on the record of Hansard, would serve no useful purpose. It is clear that no useful purpose would be served by calling another conference.
This legislation is required now in order that the provinces may be in a position to know what their fiscal positions are going to be and so that the provincial treasurers will be able to guide themselves accordingly in making their plans for the approaching fiscal year.
In conclusion, may I draw attention to some of the things that hon. members say they want to vote against? On this matter of the firm guarantees that I have spoken of, Mr. Speaker, let me say that this is the kind of provision which apparently did not occur to hon. members opposite in 1956. The fact is that if the Federal-Provincial Tax-Sharing Arrangements Act of 1956 had not been amended by parliament in 1958 five provinces would in one or more years have received

speechtext: Likewise all hon. members opposite will have their opportunity to say today whether they want the improved deal for the provinces that this measure offers, whether they want this vastly improved measure for the next five years or whether they want to deny to the provinces the benefit of these features of this new measure. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, item No. 1 on the
orders of the day reads as follows:
Consideration of a message from the Senate insisting upon its amendment to Bill C-72, an act to amend the Customs Tariff.
On July 6, as reported at page 7626 of Hansard, I stated the view of the government with regard to this matter in these words:
We shall not, as the Minister of Finance has said, accept the authority or right of the Senate to make this amendment. I hope the house will agree with that stand. The bill will be sent back to that body. If they choose to stand on what they have done this legislation, beneficial to the Canadian people, legislation that has universally been requested, can only pass out of existence, for we on our side will not accept the amendment.
The house overwhelmingly endorsed this stand in voting on the motion made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to this effect. In the circumstances I see no need of reiterating the arguments that were clearly set forth at that time. Those in the Senate who have insisted on asserting that which we regard, on the basis of constitutional practice, as an untenable constitutional position must accept responsibility for the economic consequences of their action-

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
Because of the bill of rights.

Private Bills

speakerposition: Prime Minister
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: And they must accept the blame for the thousands of jobs which, because of the action they have taken, will remain uncreated.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would remind the house first of all that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked for leave to revert to motions, to which we agreed. This was not the kind of statement that is ordinarily made on motions but is a statement which is made under other circumstances. However, in the light of the importance of the statement I do not think I should say anything at this time.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this is a strange attitude for the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) to take after having threatened the Senate earlier this year and having led the nation to believe that a particular course would be followed in the eventuality that the Senate insisted on its amendment.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Irresponsible.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: While the other place has taken this action, we can only say that we feel it is right that Canadians should have the right to appeal from a minister's decision. We think that the government itself is unable to slough off the responsibility for unemployment on the Senate-

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext:
-even though the Prime
Minister has tried to do that.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: Passing the buck to the Senate.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
speechtext: An irresponsible statement from an irresponsible source.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring before the house Bill No. S-30 which is a bill to incorporate the Equitable General Insurance Company. I admit the bill has arrived late from the other place, but since this session might be prorogued at any moment may I ask that with unanimous consent we pass now to the second reading of this measure?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext:
I have looked at this bill. It is the usual kind of bill
which would be brought forward in the circumstances had it been introduced in this house first rather than in the other place. If it is the intention of the hon. member to get second reading only, there would be no objection from this side. If, having got second reading, he wishes to go into the committee of the whole on the measure, I think, since it is now 6.15 or almost that, that we should leave the subject matter over until tomorrow when I feel sure in the light of the terms of the bill that there would be no objection from this side of the house.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: I believe the position taken by the hon. member for Laurier is a sound one. I believe this bill has been recommended by the superintendent of insurance, so we have no objection at all to the contents, and I think the procedure which has been suggested is satisfactory to us.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: I take it, then, that the house is willing to accede to the request of the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency and to read this bill the second time, waiving the rule which stands in the way of having it then referred to committee, and that it be proceeded with tomorrow.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: Will it not appear on the order paper tomorrow?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: The bill must go before the committee on banking and commerce unless, of course, the rule is suspended.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
speechtext: Could we not dispose of it in this manner? The bill might be read the second time and tomorrow we shall deal with it in committee of the whole. We wish to assist the hon. member in connection with this measure. I understand there has been some discussion on it in the Senate and that it has been approved. However, I do not think we should spend another 10 or 15 minutes in committee of the whole on the measure at this time, though there would be no objection to proceeding with it tomorrow in committee of the whole if that is the wish of the hon. member.

maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS

the second reading of the bill.
Motion agreed to and bill read the second time.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRIVATE BILLS
